teaser: The king of the Latin trap ballads: 'Taki Taki', 'Criminal', 'Diles' — Ozuna's sweet tenor and his catalog of reggaeton love songs made him the most-streamed Latin artist of his generation. His collaborations with Cardi B and DJ Snake made 'Taki Taki' a global monster.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Diles' — the ballad that made him a star. Notice how his voice stays soft even when the reggaeton beat pounds underneath.

name: Romeo Santos
teaser: The king of bachata: from Aventura's 'Obsesión' to his solo 'Propuesta Indecente', 'Eres Mía' and 'Imitadora' — Santos turned the Dominican genre into stadium-sized romance. His bilingual delivery and his catalog of love-and-betrayal songs made him the most successful bachata artist ever.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Propuesta Indecente' — the tango-tinged bachata about a naughty proposal. Notice how the bachata guitar pattern carries the whole arrangement.

name: Marc Anthony
teaser: The king of salsa: 'Vivir Mi Vida', 'Valió la Pena', 'I Need to Know' — Anthony's voice and his salsa revival albums made him the best-selling salsa artist of all time. His crossover pop era and his 2013 '3.0' — a pure salsa comeback — proved the genre's eternal relevance.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Vivir Mi Vida' — the triumphant remake of a French hit. Notice how the horns and the congas make the chorus a full congregation.

name: Héctor Lavoe
teaser: The voice of salsa: 'El Cantante', 'Periodico de Ayer', 'Todo Tiene Su Final' — Lavoe's tragic genius made him the defining singer of the Fania salsa era, chronicled in the film 'El Cantante'. His voice, sweet and broken, is the sound of the genre's golden age.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'El Cantante' — the song about the singer's own life. Notice how his voice carries both the celebration and the sorrow of salsa.

name: Tito Puente
teaser: The king of Latin jazz: 'Oye Como Va', 'Ran Kan Kan', 'Mambo No. 5' — Puente's timbales and his big-band mambos made him the ambassador of Latin music for five decades. His 'Oye Como Va' was covered by Santana to worldwide fame.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Oye Como Va' — the cha-cha that Santana made rock. Notice the timbales' answering phrase in every chorus.

name: Willie Colón
teaser: The trombone revolutionary of salsa: Colón's streetwise sound with Héctor Lavoe — 'Calle Luna Calle Sol', 'Pedro Navaja' — gave salsa its grit. His 'Siembra' with Rubén Blades remains one of the best-selling salsa albums ever, and his arrangements defined the Fania sound.

exploreAction.targetName: Willie Colón & Héctor Lavoe — Lo Mato (1973) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Calle Luna Calle Sol' — the bolero about Puerto Rico's streets. Notice how the trombones growl under the melody.

name: Chico Buarque
teaser: Brazil's poet of resistance: 'Apesar de Você', 'Construção', 'Geni e o Zepelim' — Buarque's sambas and bossa nova hid political defiance from the censorship of the dictatorship. His songwriting, with its wordplay and tenderness, makes him Brazil's greatest living lyricist.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the title track — the song about a construction worker's death, told with a metronomic, building-site rhythm. Notice how the lyrics are all in the same grammatical structure, a technical marvel.

name: Gal Costa
teaser: The voice of tropicalia: 'Baby', 'Fatal', 'Vaca Profana' — Costa's soaring, ecstatic singing made her the movement's greatest female voice, from the psychedelic 'Tropicalia' era to her bossa and rock explorations. Her death in 2022 closed a golden chapter of Brazilian music.

exploreAction.targetName: Gal Costa — Tropicalia: Ou Panis et Circencis (1968) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Baby' — Caetano Veloso's song, sung by Gal with a smile that changes the meaning. Notice how her voice glides from samba to rock without effort.

name: Maria Bethânia
teaser: The dramatic soul of Brazilian song: 'Carcará', 'Explode Coração', 'Álibi' — Bethânia's theatrical, folk-rooted singing made her one of the most powerful stage presences in MPB. Her live albums are events, her phrasing is prayer.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Carcará' — the hawk song that launched her career. Notice how her voice embodies the bird's menace and freedom.

name: Seu Jorge
teaser: The Brazilian everyman who turned Bowie into samba: his 'The Life Aquatic' soundtrack — Portuguese-language covers of David Bowie — made him a global name. His own albums mix samba, soul and MPB, and his voice is the sound of Rio's streets.

exploreAction.targetName: Seu Jorge — The Life Aquatic Studio Sessions (2005) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Starman' — Bowie in Portuguese, reinvented as samba. Notice how the acoustic guitar and the voice carry everything.

name: Tim Maia
teaser: The soul giant of Brazil: 'Não Quero Dinheiro', 'Azul da Cor do Mar', 'Primavera' — Maia brought American soul and funk to Brazil, and his 'Rational Culture' albums — recorded during his cult phase — are among the strangest and best records of the seventies. His voice is a force of nature.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Azul da Cor do Mar' — the sweet, floating opener. Then find his 'Rational Culture' records for the funk-cult masterpiece nobody expected.

name: M83
teaser: The French shoegaze-electronic symphonies of Anthony Gonzalez: 'Midnight City', 'Wait', 'Outro' — his 'Hurry Up, We're Dreaming' album is a double record of stadium-sized nostalgia. His music is the sound of every coming-of-age film montage.

exploreAction.targetName: M83 — Hurry Up, We're Dreaming (2011) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Midnight City' — the saxophone solo that appears out of nowhere. Notice how the album swings between bombast and whispered interludes.

name: CHVRCHES
teaser: The Scottish synth-pop trio: Lauren Mayberry's clear, pointed voice over the band's gleaming production — 'The Mother We Share', 'Recover', 'Clearest Blue' — made them the smartest pop act of the 2010s indie wave. Their collaboration with Robert Smith ('How Not to Drown') proved their range.

exploreAction.targetName: CHVRCHES — The Bones of What You Believe (2013) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'The Mother We Share' — the album's opening statement. Notice how the synths are arranged like guitars, with distortion and weight.

name: Alt-J
teaser: The Mercury Prize-winning math-pop trio: 'Breezeblocks', 'Tessellate', 'Left Hand Free' — their songs are built from odd meters, layered samples and Joe Newman's mumbled, half-spoken vocals. 'An Awesome Wave' sounded like nothing else in 2012 and still doesn't.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Breezeblocks' — the children's rhyme (where the wild things are) turned into a love song about violence. Notice the harpsichord and the electronic textures.

name: Two Door Cinema Club
teaser: The Northern Irish indie-disco trio: 'What You Know', 'Something Good Can Work', 'Undercover Martyn' — their bright, treble-heavy guitars and danceable basslines defined the 2010s festival sound. Their debut 'Tourist History' is a perfect summer album.

exploreAction.targetName: Two Door Cinema Club — Tourist History (2010) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'What You Know' — the guitar melody that is the whole hook. Notice how the band never needs a solo; the rhythm is the song.

name: Jungle
teaser: The London collective who made funk the future: 'Back on 74', 'Busy Earnin'', 'Time' — their choreographed videos and silky soul-funk made them the revival's most stylish act. 'Volcano' (2023) added new depth to the formula.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Back on 74' — the disco-funk anthem with the dance video everyone copied. Notice how the bass and the falsetto harmony lock together.

name: Parcels
teaser: The Australian five-piece who make disco sound hand-made: 'Overnight' (produced by Daft Punk), 'Lightenup', 'Theworstthing' — their live show, all analog instruments and one-take energy, is the reason the genre refuses to die. 'Live Vol. 1' captures the magic.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Theworstthing' — the nine-minute opener with the disco breakdown. Notice how the band's instruments all breathe together like one organism.

name: Odesza
teaser: The Seattle duo who made electronic music cinematic: 'Sun Models', 'Say My Name', 'Line of Sight' — their brass-heavy, vocal-laced productions and their 'A Moment Apart' tour with its drumline and choir made them the biggest act in melodic EDM. Their live show is a religious experience.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Line of Sight' — the choral hook and the bass drop that follows. Notice how the album alternates between club tracks and ambient interludes.

name: Ben Böhmer
teaser: The German melodic-house maestro: 'Breathing', 'Hunting', 'Cappadocia' — Böhmer's warm, organic productions (piano, strings, tape noise) made him the leading light of the Anjunadeep scene. His live shows with a grand piano on stage bridge the club and the concert hall.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Breathing' — the Nils Hoffmann remix that is more famous than the original. Notice how the piano melody floats above the kick drum.

name: Lane 8
teaser: The melodic-house purist who rejects the drop: 'Diamonds', 'Brightest Lights', 'Survive' — Daniel Goldstein's progressive house is built on long, emotional builds and pianos instead of bass drops. His 'Reviver' album and his sunrise sets have made him the genre's most reliable romantic.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'What Have You Done to Me?' — the album's centerpiece with its shifting chords. Notice how the music rewards patience: the payoffs take minutes, not seconds.

name: Jefferson Airplane
teaser: The psychedelic pioneers of San Francisco: 'Somebody to Love', 'White Rabbit', 'Volunteers' — Grace Slick's operatic vocals and the band's acid-rock attack made them the voice of 1967's Summer of Love. Their 'Surrealistic Pillow' album is the psychedelic era's essential document.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'White Rabbit' — the song built on the 'Bolero' rhythm and Alice in Wonderland imagery. Notice the fuzz guitar and the marching snare.

name: The Grateful Dead
teaser: The band that was a community: fifty years of touring, jamming and tape trading made the Dead rock's most devoted subculture. 'Casey Jones', 'Truckin'', 'Ripple' — and the live improvisations that could stretch a song for forty minutes. Jerry Garcia's guitar was the congregation's voice.

exploreAction.targetName: The Grateful Dead — American Beauty (1970) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Ripple' — the hymn-like ballad with the banjo. Then find a live 'Dark Star' and hear what the Dead were really about: improvisation as ritual.

name: Janis Joplin
teaser: The woman who sang like she was on fire: 'Piece of My Heart', 'Me and Bobby McGee', 'Cry Baby' — Joplin's raw, blues-shouting voice made her the first female rock superstar. She died of a heroin overdose at twenty-seven, days after recording her masterpiece 'Pearl'.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Me and Bobby McGee' — the Kris Kristofferson song she made her own. Notice how her voice cracks, growls and soars within a single verse.

name: The Byrds
teaser: The band that made folk rock a genre: 'Mr. Tambourine Man', 'Turn! Turn! Turn!', 'Eight Miles High' — Roger McGuinn's twelve-string Rickenbacker and the band's harmonies gave Dylan's songs electric wings. Their 'Sweetheart of the Rodeo' album even invented country rock.

exploreAction.targetName: The Byrds — Mr. Tambourine Man (1965) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the title track — the jingle-jangle guitar that defined the decade. Notice how the harmonies stack like a folk group with a rock engine.

name: The Mamas & the Papas
teaser: The California dream vocal group: 'California Dreamin'', 'Monday, Monday', 'Dream a Little Dream of Me' — John Phillips' songs and the four-part blend of the group made them the harmony kings of 1966. Their music is sunshine and melancholy in one golden package.

exploreAction.targetName: The Mamas & the Papas — If You Can Believe Your Eyes and Ears (1966) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'California Dreamin'' — the oboe intro and the four voices entering one by one. Notice how the song is about longing for a place that's also a feeling.

name: The Zombies
teaser: The baroque-pop geniuses who recorded their masterpiece after breaking up: 'Time of the Season', 'She's Not There', 'Care of Cell 44' — Rod Argent's keyboard-forward, classically trained songwriting made 'Odessey and Oracle' a late-arriving classic. Released to silence in 1968, it became one of the most loved albums of the sixties.

exploreAction.targetName: The Zombies — Odessey and Oracle (1968) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Time of the Season' — the bassline and the falsetto 'what's your name?' hook. Notice the Mellotron and the psychedelic production on 'Hung Up on a Dream'.

name: The Moody Blues
teaser: The band that fused rock and orchestra: 'Nights in White Satin', 'Tuesday Afternoon' — their 'Days of Future Passed' album, recorded with the London Festival Orchestra, invented symphonic rock. Justin Hayward's lush voice and the Mellotron made them the sound of cosmic romance.

exploreAction.targetName: The Moody Blues — Days of Future Passed (1967) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Nights in White Satin' — the song that refuses to end, with its spoken poem. Notice how the orchestra swells under the rock band.

name: Procol Harum
teaser: The one-hit wonder with the immortal hit: 'A Whiter Shade of Pale' — with its Bach-inspired organ line and its surreal lyrics — is one of the most played songs in history. Gary Brooker's gospel-tinged voice and the band's baroque rock made them much more than the single.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'A Whiter Shade of Pale' — the organ introduction is adapted from Bach's 'Air on a G String'. Notice how the lyrics remain famously meaningless and perfect.

name: Free
teaser: The British blues-rockers with the definitive guitar tone: 'All Right Now', 'Wishing Well', 'Alright Now' — Paul Kossoff's singing lead guitar and Paul Rodgers' soulful roar made Free the template for Bad Company and every British blues band after. 'All Right Now' remains a stadium staple.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'All Right Now' — the riff that never stops and the chorus that everyone knows. Notice how Kossoff bends a single note into a whole solo.

name: Bad Company
teaser: The supergroup of British blues rock: Paul Rodgers, Simon Kirke and company turned 'Can't Get Enough', 'Bad Company' and 'Feel Like Makin' Love' into the sound of the seventies arena. Their debut album is one of the best-selling rock debuts of the decade.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Can't Get Enough' — the chugging riff and Rodgers' effortless power. Notice how the band's restraint makes the chorus land.

name: The Allman Brothers Band
teaser: The band that made Southern rock a movement: Duane Allman's slide guitar, Dickey Betts' twin leads and the double-drummer attack of 'Whipping Post', 'Ramblin' Man' and the live 'At Fillmore East' — the greatest live album in rock history. Duane's death at twenty-four ended the original lineup, but the legacy never died.

exploreAction.targetName: The Allman Brothers Band — At Fillmore East (1971) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the twenty-three-minute version of 'Whipping Post' — the jam that defines the genre. Notice how the two drummers and the two guitarists weave together.

name: Steppenwolf
teaser: The band that gave bikers their anthem: 'Born to Be Wild' — with its 'heavy metal thunder' lyric — invented the genre's name and became the soundtrack of Easy Rider. 'Magic Carpet Ride' and 'The Pusher' completed their catalog of rebellion.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Born to Be Wild' — the opening riff and the 'heavy metal thunder' line. Notice how the organ doubles the guitar for a fatter sound.

name: Canned Heat
teaser: The boogie-blues revivalists of the sixties: 'Going Up the Country', 'On the Road Again', 'Let's Work Together' — their Woodstock set and their hypnotic boogie made them the soundtrack of the festival era. 'Going Up the Country' became the unofficial anthem of the whole generation.

exploreAction.targetName: Canned Heat — Living the Blues (1968) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Going Up the Country' — the song built on a Henry Thomas 1928 field recording. Notice how the flute solo makes it sound like a sunny day.

name: The Animals
teaser: The gritty R&B band from Newcastle: 'The House of the Rising Sun', 'We Gotta Get Out of This Place', 'Don't Let Me Be Misunderstood' — Eric Burdon's howling voice and Alan Price's organ made them the most soulful of the British Invasion bands. Their version of the New Orleans folk song became a worldwide number one.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'The House of the Rising Sun' — the three-minute organ-led epic recorded in one take. Notice how Burdon's voice tells the whole story.

name: The Yardbirds
teaser: The band that launched three guitar legends: Eric Clapton, Jeff Beck and Jimmy Page all passed through its lineup. 'For Your Love', 'Heart Full of Soul', 'Over Under Sideways Down' — their experiments with feedback and Middle Eastern scales made them the bridge between blues rock and psychedelia.

exploreAction.targetName: The Yardbirds — Roger the Engineer (1966) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Over Under Sideways Down' — the driving riff and Jeff Beck's fuzz tone. Notice how the band's sound anticipates Led Zeppelin by two years.

name: Small Faces
teaser: The mod masterpiece makers: 'Itchycoo Park', 'Tin Soldier', 'Lazy Sunday' — Steve Marriott's soulful shriek and Ronnie Lane's songwriting made them the most exciting British band of the mod era. Their 'Ogdens' Nut Gone Flake' concept album is a psychedelic treasure.

exploreAction.targetName: Small Faces — Ogdens' Nut Gone Flake (1968) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Itchycoo Park' — the song with the flanger effect that sounds like swirling. Notice how Marriott's voice switches from angelic to raw in one line.

name: Humble Pie
teaser: The heavy blues supergroup: Peter Frampton and Steve Marriott's twin-guitar front line — 'I Don't Need No Doctor', '30 Days in the Hole', 'Rockin' the Fillmore' — made Humble Pie the loudest, greasiest band of the early seventies. Their live album 'Performance: Rockin' the Fillmore' is a blues-rock landmark.

exploreAction.targetName: Humble Pie — Performance: Rockin' the Fillmore (1971) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'I Don't Need No Doctor' — the seventeen-minute live version with the dual-guitar battle. Notice how Marriott's scream and Frampton's wah-wah trade blows.

name: Ten Years After
teaser: The Woodstock guitar heroes: Alvin Lee's machine-gun speed on 'I'm Going Home' — a twelve-minute improvisation at Woodstock that made him the festival's breakout star. 'I'd Love to Change the World' showed the gentler side of the same lightning fingers.

exploreAction.targetName: Ten Years After — A Space in Time (1971) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'I'd Love to Change the World' — the acoustic-electric anthem with the famous fuzz guitar solo. Notice how the song's message and its riff are equally memorable.

name: Bill Withers
teaser: The soul everyman who walked away at the top: 'Ain't No Sunshine', 'Lean on Me', 'Grandma's Hands', 'Lovely Day' — Withers' warm, plain-spoken songs are among the most covered in history. He quit the music industry in 1985 and never looked back, leaving a flawless catalog.

exploreAction.targetName: Bill Withers — Just As I Am (1971) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Ain't No Sunshine' — the song with the famous 'I know' repetition. Notice how the bass and the voice carry everything.

name: Donny Hathaway
teaser: The soul genius with the voice of velvet steel: 'A Song for You', 'The Ghetto', 'This Christmas' — Hathaway's gospel-trained piano and his duets with Roberta Flack made him one of the most gifted artists of the seventies. His death at thirty-three, in a fall from a hotel window, remains a haunting mystery.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'A Song for You' — the live version where his voice seems to reach beyond the song. Notice how the piano and voice are in constant dialogue.

name: Roberta Flack
teaser: The quiet storm pioneer: 'Killing Me Softly with His Song', 'The First Time Ever I Saw Your Face', 'Where Is the Love' — Flack's jazz-trained restraint and her nightly care for every phrase made her the most elegant voice of seventies soul. 'Killing Me Softly' was a global phenomenon twice over (Fugees covered it).

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'The First Time Ever I Saw Your Face' — the song that took three years to become a hit, after it appeared in a film. Notice how the piano builds slowly, then the strings arrive.

name: Chic
teaser: The band that made disco smart: Nile Rodgers' chicken-scratch guitar and Bernard Edwards' bass — 'Le Freak', 'Good Times', 'Everybody Dance' — turned the dancefloor into a laboratory. 'Good Times' was sampled by Sugarhill Gang ('Rapper's Delight') and Queen ('Another One Bites the Dust'), seeding both hip-hop and pop's future.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Good Times' — the bassline that launched a thousand samples. Notice how the arrangement leaves space for every instrument to shine.

name: Nile Rodgers
teaser: The guitarist-producer who made the sound of pop: from Chic's 'Le Freak' to Madonna's 'Like a Virgin', David Bowie's 'Let's Dance' and Daft Punk's 'Get Lucky' — Rodgers' 'chucking' guitar style and his refusal to repeat himself have spanned five decades of number ones. He has made the same chord four decades sound new every time.

exploreAction.targetName: Nile Rodgers — Get Lucky (2013) with Daft Punk — and Chic's Le Freak (1978)
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Get Lucky' — his guitar is the song's center. Notice how his signature style — the tight, syncopated 'chuck' — carries the groove without a bassline.

name: George Benson
teaser: The guitarist who sang his way to the top: 'Give Me the Night', 'On Broadway', 'This Masquerade' — Benson's jazz guitar virtuosity and his soulful singing made him the most successful jazz-crossover artist ever. His 'Breezin'' album went platinum, a first for jazz.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'This Masquerade' — the scat-singing guitar duet where he sings and plays the same line. Notice how his guitar tone is warm as a voice.

name: Bobby Womack
teaser: The soul survivor: 'Across 110th Street', 'If You Think You're Lonely Now', 'Lookin' for a Love' — Womack wrote for the Rolling Stones ('It's All Over Now'), played guitar for everyone, and recorded some of the grittiest soul of the seventies. His comeback album 'The Bravest Man in the Universe' was nominated for a Mercury Prize.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'If You Think You're Lonely Now' — the song Drake sampled for 'Marvin's Room'. Notice how Womack's voice sounds like it has lived every word.

name: Alison Krauss
teaser: The bluegrass angel: with her band Union Station, Krauss's crystalline soprano and her fiddle playing made 'When You Say Nothing at All', 'Down to the River to Pray' (O Brother, Where Art Thou?) and the 'Raising Sand' collaboration with Robert Plant into crossover classics. She is the most awarded female artist in Grammy history.

exploreAction.targetName: Alison Krauss & Union Station — New Favorite (2001) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'The Lucky One' — her voice over the band's immaculate acoustic playing. Notice how quiet the mix is, letting every note ring.

name: Dwight Yoakam
teaser: The honky-tonk revivalist who brought the Buck Owens sound back: 'Guitars, Cadillacs', 'Honky Tonk Man', 'A Thousand Miles from Nowhere' — Yoakam's tight pants, bucking-bronco stage moves and his low, lonesome voice made him the sharpest country traditionalist of the eighties.

exploreAction.targetName: Dwight Yoakam — Guitars, Cadillacs, Etc., Etc. (1986) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the title track — the Bakersfield sound with a modern attack. Notice how his voice yodels and cracks with pure country feeling.

name: Steve Earle
teaser: The outlaw's heir: 'Guitar Town', 'Copperhead Road', 'The Revolution Starts Now' — Earle's hard-country songwriting and his prison-time, sobriety and politics made him country's most uncompromising voice. His albums are dispatches from the American working class.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the title track — the heavy, electric Irish-tinged stomp. Notice how the album mixes folk ballads and full-bore rock without losing its country spine.

name: Townes Van Zandt
teaser: The songwriter's songwriter: 'Pancho and Lefty', 'If I Needed You', 'Waiting Around to Die' — Van Zandt wrote some of the most devastating songs in American music, lived a hard-scrabble life of addiction, and was idolized by Steve Earle, Guy Clark and John Prine. His music is the purest distillation of the Texas troubadour tradition.

exploreAction.targetName: Townes Van Zandt — The Late Great Townes Van Zandt (1972) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Pancho and Lefty' — the song about two outlaws that everyone has covered. Notice how his voice, quiet and cracked, tells the story without judgment.

name: Guy Clark
teaser: The craftsman of Texas songwriting: 'Desperados Waiting for a Train', 'L.A. Freeway', 'The Randall Knife' — Clark's songs are hand-built like the guitars he made, precise and warm. He mentored Steve Earle, Rodney Crowell and a generation of Nashville writers from his kitchen table.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Desperados Waiting for a Train' — the song about the man who was like a grandfather. Notice how the details (the car, the Christmas presents) do the emotional work.

name: Lucinda Williams
teaser: The queen of the singer-songwriter underground: 'Passionate Kisses', 'Car Wheels on a Gravel Road', 'Righteously' — Williams's blend of country, blues and rock and her exacting, literary lyrics took eighteen years to make her breakthrough album. It won the Grammy and changed Americana forever.

exploreAction.targetName: Lucinda Williams — Car Wheels on a Gravel Road (1998) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the title track — her memory-song about the South. Notice how her voice, Southern and full, makes every line feel confessed.

name: Billy Strings
teaser: The bluegrass prodigy who turned the genre into a jam-band phenomenon: 'Dust in a Baggie', 'Away from the Mire', 'Meet Me at the Creek' — Strings' lightning flatpicking and his psychedelic, improvisational live shows have made him the biggest new force in acoustic music. He won the Grammy for Best Bluegrass Album in 2021.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Dust in a Baggie' — the true-story song about a meth arrest, played at bluegrass speed. Notice how the banjo and guitar trade fire.

name: Sierra Ferrell
teaser: The Americana sensation with the voice of an old record: 'In Dreams', 'Why'd Ya Do It', 'The Sea of Darkness' — Ferrell's vintage-sounding songs, recorded with her band of virtuoso string players, made 'Long Time Coming' one of the most acclaimed debuts of the 2020s. She performs in a world that feels a century old.

exploreAction.targetName: Sierra Ferrell — Long Time Coming (2021) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'In Dreams' — the waltz with the old-time fiddle. Notice how her voice cracks and swoops like a 78 rpm record come to life.

name: Rhiannon Giddens
teaser: The banjo historian who reclaimed Black roots music: from the Carolina Chocolate Drops to her solo work and her opera 'Omar', Giddens' scholarship and her soaring voice have rewritten American music history. Her solo albums 'Tomorrow Is My Turn' and 'You're the One' are both lesson and celebration.

exploreAction.targetName: Rhiannon Giddens — You're the One (2023) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'You Louisiana Man' — the danceable, banjo-driven opener. Notice how the album pulls from blues, country, gospel and folk in one set.

name: John Legend
teaser: The modern soul standard-bearer: 'All of Me', 'Ordinary People', 'Green Light' — Legend's church-trained piano and his songwriting made him one of the most consistent hitmakers of the 2000s. His 'All of Me' (written for his wife Chrissy Teigen) is one of the most-streamed love songs ever.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Ordinary People' — the slow-burn piano ballad that made him a star. Notice how the verses are nearly spoken, building to the full-voice chorus.

name: Ne-Yo
teaser: The songwriter's songwriter who became the voice: 'So Sick', 'Because of You', 'Closer' — Ne-Yo wrote hits for Beyoncé, Rihanna and Mario before his own debut made him a star. His sleek R&B and his dance-pop pivot ('Closer') defined the late 2000s sound.

exploreAction.targetName: Ne-Yo — In My Own Words (2006) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'So Sick' — the breakup hit built on a simple piano loop. Notice how his smooth falsetto carries the melody.

name: Chris Brown
teaser: The most decorated R&B performer of his generation: 'Run It!', 'Kiss Kiss', 'Forever', 'No Guidance' — Brown's singing, dancing and catalog of hits are undeniable, even as his personal controversies continue to define his public story. His dance moves set the standard for modern pop performance.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Forever' — the wedding-anthem smash. Notice how the album's production by The-Dream and others keeps the R&B glossy and huge.

name: The-Dream
teaser: The R&B architect behind a decade of hits: 'Shawty Is a Ten', 'I Love Your Girl', and his songwriting for Rihanna ('Umbrella'), Beyoncé ('Single Ladies') and Mariah Carey — The-Dream's falsetto and his lyrical wit made him the most influential R&B writer of the 2000s. His 'Love Hate' album is a cult classic.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Shawty Is a Ten' — the slow-burning groove. Notice how his falsetto phrases ride the beat like a second percussion part.

name: Khalid
teaser: The teen heartthrob of modern soul: 'Location', 'Young Dumb & Broke', 'Talk' — Khalid's debut, recorded at seventeen, made him the voice of a generation's soft-boy melancholy. His warm, easy delivery and his streaming-era dominance made him one of the biggest R&B stars of the late 2010s.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Location' — the GPS love song with the minimal beat. Notice how his voice stays conversational, never straining, even on the biggest hooks.

name: Leon Bridges
teaser: The retro-soul revival's most convincing voice: 'Coming Home', 'River', 'Beyond' — Bridges' 1950s-style croon and his sharp suits made his debut an instant classic. His later albums, 'Good Thing' and 'Gold-Diggers Sound', pushed the vintage sound into modern pop without losing the warmth.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Coming Home' — the doo-wop-inspired opener. Notice how the production is period-authentic: tape hiss, reverb and a live band.

name: Brent Faiyaz
teaser: The velvet-voiced R&B anti-hero: 'Trust', 'Clouded', 'Gravity' — Faiyaz's hushed, luxurious delivery and his genre-bending production made him the leading light of the 2020s R&B underground. His 'Wasteland' album debuted at number one A string of mixtapes — Into, Lost, and Fuck the World — built a devoted cult following before his debut album made him a genuine star.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Gravity' — the DJ Dahi-produced centerpiece with the layered harmonies. Notice how his voice stays low and intimate over the trap-inflected beat.

name: Lucky Daye
teaser: The New Orleans R&B heir: 'Roll Some Mo', 'Over', 'NWA' — Daye's gospel-raised voice and his jazz-informed arrangements made 'Painted' one of the most acclaimed R&B debuts of 2019. His 'Candydrip' follow-up deepened the sound.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Roll Some Mo' — the percussion-forward opener with the slinky bassline. Notice how his voice stretches and slides over the groove.

name: Snoh Aalegra
teaser: The Swedish-American soul singer with the timeless voice: 'I Want You Around', 'Dying 4 Your Love', 'Fool for You' — Aalegra's debut 'Ugh, Those Feels Again' and its follow-up 'Temporary Highs in the Violet Skies' made her the most critically beloved new R&B voice of the late 2010s.

exploreAction.targetName: Snoh Aalegra — Ugh, Those Feels Again (2019) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'I Want You Around' — the Michael Jackson-esque swing. Notice how the production, by No I.D., frames her voice like a vintage soul record.

name: Omar Apollo
teaser: The genre-hopping Mexican-American heartthrob: 'Evergreen', 'Killing Me', 'Ivory' — Apollo's blend of R&B, funk, indie and Spanish-language ballads made him one of the most exciting young artists of the 2020s. His 'Ivory' debut announced a star with range to burn.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Evergreen' — the aching ballad with the string section. Notice how his voice moves between English and Spanish within the same song.

name: Trey Songz
teaser: The smooth-voiced R&B mainstay: 'Can't Help but Wait', 'Say Aah', 'Neighbors Know My Name' — Songz's bedroom ballads and his party anthems made him a consistent hitmaker from the late 2000s into the 2020s. His 'Ready' and 'Passion, Pain & Pleasure' albums are R&B essentials.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Say Aah' — the club anthem with the Fabolous verse. Notice how his voice moves from smooth tenor to falsetto on the hook.

name: Mario
teaser: The teenage R&B prodigy who grew up on the charts: 'Just a Friend 2002', 'Let Me Love You', 'How Could You' — Mario's debut made him a star at fifteen, and his 'Let Me Love You' became one of the most played R&B songs of the 2000s. His voice, a rich, agile tenor, has only deepened.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Let Me Love You' — the Ne-Yo-penned ballad that topped charts worldwide. Notice how the production's minimal beat lets his voice carry the melody.

name: Roddy Ricch
teaser: The Compton trap poet: 'The Box', 'High Fashion', 'Late at Night' — Ricch's debut 'Please Excuse Me for Being Antisocial' went platinum and 'The Box' became the longest-running number-one of 2020. His melodic, introspective trap made him the defining voice of the pandemic-era charts.

exploreAction.targetName: Roddy Ricch — Please Excuse Me for Being Antisocial (2019) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'The Box' — the beat-switching viral smash with the humming hook. Notice how his voice morphs between singing and rapping in the same bar.

name: Lil Baby
teaser: The trap star with the conscience: 'Drip Too Hard', 'Yes Indeed', 'The Bigger Picture' — Lil Baby's melodic flow and his protest anthem (written after George Floyd's murder) made him the most important mainstream rapper of the early 2020s. 'My Turn' was the best-selling rap album of 2020.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'The Bigger Picture' — the protest song that won him Grammys and respect. Notice how the production by 30 Roc frames his voice like a documentary narrator.

name: Lil Durk
teaser: The voice of Chicago drill's emotional wing: 'Viral Moment', 'All Love', 'Broadway Girls' — Durk's vulnerable, melodic drill and his collaborations with Lil Baby made him one of the most streamed rappers of the 2020s. His 'The Voice' and '7220' albums turned pain into platinum.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Viral Moment' — the introspective opener about loss. Notice how his autotuned croon carries grief over the drill beat.

name: DaBaby
teaser: The Charlotte rapper with the machine-gun delivery: 'Suge', 'BOP', 'Rockstar' — DaBaby's explosive flow and his charisma made him the biggest breakout rapper of 2019-2020. 'Rockstar' was the number-one song of the summer of 2020 before his public controversies derailed the run.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Suge' — the drill-inflected smash with the deadpan hook. Notice how his flow accelerates and stops on a dime.

name: Patti Smith
teaser: The poet laureate of punk: 'Gloria', 'Because the Night', 'People Have the Power' — Smith's 'Horses' album, with its Robert Mapplethorpe cover and its opening line 'Jesus died for somebody's sins but not mine', announced that punk could be literature. Her memoir 'Just Kids' won the National Book Award.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the opening of 'Gloria' — the famous 'Jesus died...' spoken intro before the riff crashes in. Notice how the band (with Lenny Kaye) plays garage rock beneath her poetry.

name: Television
teaser: The guitar-band's guitar band: Tom Verlaine and Richard Lloyd's interlocking, jazz-informed guitar lines on 'Marquee Moon' — the eleven-minute title track — made them the most sophisticated band of the CBGB scene. Their 1977 debut is the benchmark for twin-guitar interplay.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the title track — the dual guitar solos that trade and weave for minutes. Notice how every part of the song is composed, not improvised.

name: The New York Dolls
teaser: The glam-punk originals: 'Personality Crisis', 'Jet Boy', 'Looking for a Kiss' — the Dolls' trashy, transgressive rock and their drag-queen glamour scandalized 1973 and inspired everyone from the Sex Pistols to Kiss. David Johansen's sneer and Johnny Thunders' sloppy genius made them the missing link.

exploreAction.targetName: The New York Dolls — New York Dolls (1973) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Personality Crisis' — the song that defined the band's chaos. Notice how the Rolling Stones' swagger is pushed into something uglier and freer.

name: Big Star
teaser: The power-pop perfectionists who sold almost nothing and influenced everyone: Alex Chilton's 'September Gurls', 'In the Street', 'Thirteen' — their two 1972 albums became the holy grail of sixties-style melodic rock. R.E.M., the Replacements and a generation of indie bands built their sound on Big Star's bones.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Thirteen' — the teenage-love song that makes adulthood sound like a fall. Notice how Chilton's voice and the Byrds-like jangle carry the melody.

name: The Replacements
teaser: The sloppy, brilliant anti-rock stars: Paul Westerberg's 'Unsatisfied', 'Bastards of Young', 'I Will Dare' — the Replacements made chaos a genre, from punk ragers to heartbreaking ballads, often in the same song. They are the godfathers of American indie rock, and they never once looked like it.

exploreAction.targetName: The Replacements — Let It Be (1984) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Unsatisfied' — the album's quiet, devastating center. Notice how the band's punk noise makes the ballads land harder.

name: Hüsker Dü
teaser: The Minneapolis trio who made punk melodic: 'Don't Want to Know If You Are Lonely', 'Makes No Sense at All' — Bob Mould's roaring guitar and Grant Hart's pop instincts turned three-minute hardcore into anthems. Their double album 'Zen Arcade' is the gateway between punk and alternative rock.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Something I Learned Today' — the forty-five-second opener. Notice how the album's noise resolves into the acoustic closer 'Recurring Dreams'.

name: Dinosaur Jr.
teaser: The loudest quiet band in indie: J Mascis's towering fuzz guitar and his mumbling, melancholy vocals — 'Feel the Pain', 'Start Choppin'', 'Freak Scene' — made Dinosaur Jr. the template for nineties alt-rock. Their reunion albums proved the formula still works.

exploreAction.targetName: Dinosaur Jr. — You're Living All Over Me (1987) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Freak Scene' — the song that invented slacker rock. Notice how the fuzz tone swallows the whole mix, with Mascis's voice floating on top.

name: Pavement
teaser: The kings of slacker indie: Stephen Malkmus's wry, unplaceable vocals and the band's scruffy genius — 'Cut Your Hair', 'Summer Babe', 'Gold Soundz' — made Pavement the most beloved band of the nineties underground. Their 'Crooked Rain, Crooked Rain' is the definitive indie album.

exploreAction.targetName: Pavement — Crooked Rain, Crooked Rain (1994) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Gold Soundz' — the song that defines their warm, messy charm. Notice how the guitars sound almost out of tune but perfectly placed.

name: Guided by Voices
teaser: The lo-fi hit machine: Robert Pollard's four-track demos — 'I Am a Scientist', 'Gold Star for Robot Boy', 'Motor Away' — produced literally hundreds of songs, many under two minutes, recorded on cheap tape with a rotating cast. Their 'Bee Thousand' album made basement recording a legitimate art form.

exploreAction.targetName: Guided by Voices — Bee Thousand (1994) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the whole album — 20 songs in 36 minutes, many just guitar and voice. Notice how the tape hiss and the pop melodies make each tiny song feel epic.

name: Yo La Tengo
teaser: The shape-shifting trio who can do anything: 'Autumn Sweater', 'Nuclear War', 'I Heard You Looking' — from gentle folk to eleven-minute noise jams, Yo La Tengo have been indie's most dependable institution since 1984. Ira Kaplan and Georgia Hubley are indie rock's first couple.

exploreAction.targetName: Yo La Tengo — I Can Hear the Heart Beating as One (1997) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Autumn Sweater' — the organ and the slow, gorgeous groove. Notice how the album swings between whisper-quiet songs and full noise.

name: Built to Spill
teaser: The Boise guitar heroes: Doug Martsch's epic, sprawling songs — 'Carry the Zero', 'The Plan', 'Stop the Fuckin' Car' — made Built to Spill the standard-bearer of nineties indie rock. Their guitar solos are patient, melodic mountains that take five minutes to climb.

exploreAction.targetName: Built to Spill — Perfect from Now On (1997) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Carry the Zero' — the riff that builds for minutes before releasing. Notice how Martsch's voice, thin and urgent, sits above the guitars.

name: The Breeders
teaser: The Pixies' bassist's other band: Kim Deal's 'Cannonball', 'Divine Hammer', 'Safari' — the Breeders' 'Last Splash' went platinum on the strength of Deal's slacker-cool hooks. 'Cannonball' remains the greatest bassline in nineties alternative rock The band's loud-quiet dynamics and Kim Deal's detached, cool vocals turned a side project into one of the definitive alt-rock records of the decade.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Cannonball' — the riff that made MTV play it on repeat. Notice how Deal's vocal, doubled and deadpan, floats over the fuzz bass.

name: The xx
teaser: The minimalist trio who made less sound like everything: 'Crystalised', 'VCR', 'Angels' — the xx's music is built from silence, bass and Romy Madley Croft's and Oliver Sim's intertwining voices. Their self-titled debut won the Mercury Prize and their 'Coexist' and 'I See You' albums kept the formula fresh.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Crystalised' — the two voices trade the melody as if sharing a secret. Notice how the album leaves empty space where other bands pile sound.

name: Foals
teaser: The Oxford math-rockers who became festival kings: 'Spanish Sahara', 'My Number', 'Mountain at My Gates' — Foals' evolution from jerky, danceable post-punk to massive anthems made them the biggest British indie band of the 2010s. Their live shows are legendary for their communal energy.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'My Number' — the dance-punk hit with the disco bassline. Notice how 'Inhaler' builds its guitar riff for two minutes before detonating.

name: America
teaser: The soft-rock trio who conquered the charts with harmonies: 'A Horse with No Name', 'Ventura Highway', 'Sister Golden Hair' — America's gentle, Laurel Canyon-informed folk-rock made them one of the biggest acts of the seventies. Their catalog is the soundtrack of American highways.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'A Horse with No Name' — the song about the desert that everyone misheard. Notice how the acoustic guitar pattern never changes, and the song never needs it to.

name: Bread
teaser: The soft-rock balladeers: 'Make It with You', 'If', 'Everything I Own' — David Gates's honeyed voice and the band's warm arrangements made Bread the soundtrack of seventies romance. Their ballads are among the most played slow songs of the decade.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Make It with You' — the smooth opener with the organ and the strings. Notice how the simplicity of the melody makes it immortal.

name: Oasis
teaser: The last great British rock band: Noel Gallagher's anthems — 'Wonderwall', 'Don't Look Back in Anger', 'Live Forever' — and the brotherly warfare of the Gallagher siblings made Oasis the biggest band in Britain since the Beatles. Their 'Definitely Maybe' and '(What's the Story) Morning Glory?' defined the Britpop era.

exploreAction.targetName: Oasis — (What's the Story) Morning Glory? (1995) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Wonderwall' — the song Noel wrote about his then-girlfriend and that everyone else has covered. Notice how Liam's sneer makes the melody feel like a challenge.

name: Suede
teaser: The band that started Britpop: Brett Anderson's androgynous swagger and Bernard Butler's glam-tinged guitars — 'Animal Nitrate', 'Beautiful Ones', 'Trash' — made Suede's debut the fastest-selling debut in British history. They were the art-school conscience of the movement.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Animal Nitrate' — the glam-rock riff and the louche vocal. Notice how the band's sound mixes Bowie, the Smiths and a distinctly British sleaze.

name: Pulp
teaser: Jarvis Cocker's kitchen-sink genius: 'Common People', 'Disco 2000', 'Sorted for E's & Wizz' — Pulp turned Sheffield's working-class stories into disco-funk anthems, and their 'Different Class' album is the definitive Britpop record. Cocker's stage moves and his spoken-word verses made him the movement's sharpest wit.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Common People' — the seven-minute anthem about class tourism. Notice how the disco beat makes the anger danceable.

name: Primal Scream
teaser: The band that swallowed every genre: from indie-pop to acid-house — 'Loaded', 'Movin' on Up', 'Rocks' — Primal Scream's 'Screamadelica' album, made with dance producers, fused rock and house into something new. Bobby Gillespie has kept reinventing for three decades.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Loaded' — the song built on a Peter Fonda spoken-word sample and a house beat. Notice how the gospel vocals and the acid house collide.

name: The Stone Roses
teaser: The Manchester legends who changed British guitar music: 'I Wanna Be Adored', 'Fools Gold', 'Waterfall' — the Stone Roses fused sixties pop melodies with acid-house grooves, and their 1989 debut is considered the greatest British album of its era. Their 1990 Spike Island concert became a myth.

exploreAction.targetName: The Stone Roses — The Stone Roses (1989) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Fools Gold' — the funky, beat-driven centerpiece with the wah-wah guitar. Notice how the bassline and the drums carry the song while the guitar floats.

name: Ride
teaser: The shoegaze pioneers of Oxford: 'Vapour Trail', 'Leave Them All Behind', 'Taste' — Ride's swirling twin guitars and their 1990 debut 'Nowhere' defined the genre's early sound. Their reunion albums, beginning with 'This Is Not a Safe Place', proved the drone still works.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Vapour Trail' — the album's most melodic moment. Notice how the two guitars weave a single hypnotic pattern.

name: Elastica
teaser: The post-punk minimalists of Britpop: 'Connection', 'Stutter', 'Line Up' — Justine Frischmann's band (ex-Suede) made an album of short, wired, Wire-inspired songs that sold over a million copies. Their debut is the sharpest punk record of the Britpop era.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Connection' — the two-chord masterpiece with the Motorik beat. Notice how the song is built almost entirely from riff and repetition.

name: Supergrass
teaser: The schoolboy geniuses of Britpop: 'Alright', 'Going Out', 'Richard III' — recorded when they were teenagers, Supergrass's 'I Should Coco' was a burst of pure, hooky energy. Their later albums ('In It for the Money', 'The Road to Rouen') showed the ambition under the grin.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Alright' — the summer anthem that defined 1995. Notice how the band's youth is the whole point: fast, funny and fearless.

name: Manic Street Preachers
teaser: The politicized poets of Welsh rock: 'A Design for Life', 'Motorcycle Emptiness', 'If You Tolerate This Your Children Will Be Next' — the Manics' sloganeering, glam-influenced rock and the disappearance of lyricist Richey Edwards made them one of rock's most fascinating and haunted bands.

exploreAction.targetName: Manic Street Preachers — Everything Must Go (1996) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'A Design for Life' — the orchestral anthem about working-class dignity. Notice how the lyrics quote architecture and philosophy in the same breath.

name: The Libertines
teaser: The ragged geniuses of the 2000s London scene: 'Time for Heroes', 'Can't Stand Me Now', 'Up the Bracket' — Pete Doherty and Carl Barât's shared songwriting and their chaotic, drug-addled friendship made the Libertines the most romantic band of their era. Their influence on British indie is immeasurable.

exploreAction.targetName: The Libertines — Up the Bracket (2002) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Time for Heroes' — the anthem about the two singers' own story. Notice how the band's raggedness is the charm: they sound like they might fall apart at any second.

name: Franz Ferdinand
teaser: The dance-rock revivalists: 'Take Me Out', 'Do You Want To', 'This Fire' — Alex Kapranos's band made the 2000s feel like the eighties again, with angular guitars and disco-ready choruses. Their debut won the Mercury Prize and made them global stars.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Take Me Out' — the song with two halves: the stalker verse and the disco chorus. Notice how the rhythm section locks into a funk groove.

name: Bloc Party
teaser: The post-punk intellectuals of the 2000s: 'Banquet', 'Helicopter', 'This Modern Love' — Kele Okereke's distinctive voice and the band's sharp, tense guitar sound made 'Silent Alarm' a landmark of the era. Their later albums explored electronic and more experimental territory.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Banquet' — the frantic, stuttering opener. Notice how the guitars and drums interlock like a machine built for dancing.

name: Wolf Alice
teaser: The modern British rock standard-bearers: 'Moaning Lisa Smile', 'Don't Delete the Kisses', 'The Last Man on Earth' — Wolf Alice's range, from whisper-quiet shoegaze to full metal rage, won them the Mercury Prize in 2018 for 'Visions of a Life'. Ellie Rowsell is one of the great current rock voices.

exploreAction.targetName: Wolf Alice — Visions of a Life (2017) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Don't Delete the Kisses' — the love song about texting, with the beautiful key change. Notice how the album's noise and tenderness share the same DNA.

name: Sam Fender
teaser: The Geordie Springsteen: 'Seventeen Going Under', 'Hypersonic Missiles', 'Will We Talk?' — Fender's sax-laced, working-class anthems made him the biggest new British rock star of the 2020s. His 'Seventeen Going Under' album is a masterpiece of kitchen-sink storytelling.

exploreAction.targetName: Sam Fender — Seventeen Going Under (2021) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the title track — the story of his teenage years, built on a Springsteen-sized chorus. Notice how the saxophone adds the northern English soul.

name: Big Sean
teaser: The Detroit workhorse: 'Guap', 'I Don't Fuck with You', 'Bounce Back' — Big Sean's punchline-heavy flow and his Kanye West mentorship made him a consistent hitmaker through the 2010s. His 'Dark Sky Paradise' and 'I Decided.' albums defined his confident, g-funk-tinged sound.

exploreAction.targetName: Big Sean — Dark Sky Paradise (2015) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'I Don't Fuck with You' — the Kanye-assisted anthem with the E-40 hook. Notice how Sean's double-time flow packs three punchlines per bar.

name: Wale
teaser: The wordy D.C. rapper: 'Lotus Flower Bomb', 'Ambition', 'Bad' — Wale's go-go-influenced flow and his literate, introspective lyrics made him the DMV's ambassador to mainstream rap. His 'The Album About Nothing' (with Jerry Seinfeld) is his most ambitious work.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Bad' — the Tiara Thomas duet that became a crossover hit. Notice how his voice shifts from boastful to tender mid-verse.

name: Logic
teaser: The Maryland fast-rapping intellectual: '1-800-273-8255', 'Homicide', 'Everybody' — Logic's debut 'Under Pressure' announced a technician, and his suicide-prevention anthem made him a cultural force. His 'No Pressure' farewell (since reversed) showed the full range of his skills.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the title track — the nine-minute opener about his rise. Notice the references to his own career and the blazing technical flow.

name: Joyner Lucas
teaser: The Worcester storyteller: 'Ross Capicchioni', 'I'm Not Racist', 'ISIS' — Lucas's narrative raps and his controversial, provocative videos made him one of hip-hop's most talked-about new voices. His 'ADHD' album balanced the storytelling with melodic hits.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'I'm Not Racist' — the two-sided conversation between a white man and a Black man. Notice how the song ends by revealing they're the same person.

name: G-Eazy
teaser: The slick-talking Bay Area swaggerer: 'Me, Myself & I', 'No Limit', 'Him & I' — Gerald Earl Gillum's mix of mack-culture charisma and pop hooks made him a consistent hitmaker of the mid-2010s. His 'When It's Dark Out' album went platinum.

exploreAction.targetName: G-Eazy — When It's Dark Out (2015) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Me, Myself & I' — the Bebe Rexha duet about fame's loneliness. Notice how the vintage samples and his smooth delivery hide the melancholy.

name: Polo G
teaser: The Chicago storyteller with the melodic flow: 'Finer Things', 'RAPSTAR', 'Martin & Gina' — Polo G's debut 'Die a Legend' and its follow-up 'The GOAT' made him one of the most streamed rappers of 2020. His songs about the streets and his brother's death carry real weight.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'RAPSTAR' — the auto-tuned, melodic hit that topped charts. Notice how the album alternates between drill energy and ballad vulnerability.

name: Lil Tjay
teaser: The melodic drill crooner of the Bronx: 'Brothers', 'F.N.', 'Calling My Phone' — Tjay's singing-rapping style made him one of the most streamed new artists of 2019-2020. His 2022 shooting and recovery gave his comeback an extra layer of realness.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'F.N.' — the auto-tuned melodrama about trust. Notice how his voice slides between rap and song without breaking the mood.

name: A Boogie wit da Hoodie
teaser: The Highbridge crooner: 'Drowning', 'Look Back at It', 'Mood Swings' — A Boogie's Auto-Tuned, melodic New York sound made him one of the most streamed rappers of the late 2010s. His 'Hoodie SZN' album is the sound of the city's melodic wave.

exploreAction.targetName: A Boogie wit da Hoodie — Hoodie SZN (2018) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Drowning' — the Kodak Black-featuring anthem about the streets. Notice how his voice stays high and light over the hard beat.

name: GloRilla
teaser: The Memphis breakout with the stadium-sized hooks: 'F.N.F. (Let's Go)', 'Tomorrow 2', 'Yeah Glo!' — GloRilla's booming voice and her anthems of independence made her the most exciting new rapper of 2022. Her 'Ehhthang Ehhthang' era kept the momentum.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'F.N.F. (Let's Go)' — the viral anthem about cutting off fake friends. Notice how her voice is the whole hook: no melody needed.

name: Latto
teaser: The Atlanta queen: 'Big Energy', 'Put It on Da Floor', 'Lottery' — Latto won The Rap Game at sixteen and spent years grinding before her 2021 breakout. Her confident, hook-heavy trap made her one of the biggest female rappers of the 2020s.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Big Energy' — the Mariah Carey-sampling hit with the disco bounce. Notice how her flow rides the sample's nostalgia into something new.

name: Saweetie
teaser: The Bay Area ice queen: 'Icy Grl', 'Tap In', 'Best Friend' — Saweetie's TikTok-driven viral hits and her 'Pretty Bitch Music' persona made her one of the most recognizable new rappers of 2020. Her features and her fashion line turned her into a brand.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Best Friend' — the Doja Cat duet about female friendship. Notice how her delivery is confident and playful, built for clips.

name: Coi Leray
teaser: The Jersey-bred shape-shifter: 'No More Parties', 'BIG PURR (Prrdd)', 'Players' — Coi's hooky, unpredictable music made her one of the most streamed new artists of 2021-2022. 'Players' sampled Grandmaster Flash and became a global hit.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Players' — the Grandmaster Flash remake that topped charts. Notice how she makes an old-school breakbeat sound brand new.

name: Sexyy Red
teaser: The St. Louis shock jock of rap: 'Pound Town', 'SkeeYee', 'Rich Baby Daddy' — Sexyy Red's unapologetic, absurd, meme-ready music made her the defining internet rapper of 2023. Her collaborations with Drake ('Rich Baby Daddy') took her viral energy mainstream.

exploreAction.targetName: Sexyy Red — Hood Hottest Princess (2023) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'SkeeYee' — the chanted hook that filled every club. Notice how her delivery is pure attitude, no polish needed.

name: NLE Choppa
teaser: The Memphis teenager with the breakout debut: 'Shotta Flow', 'Camelot', 'Walk Em Down' — Choppa was the youngest rapper to chart with a viral hit, and his pivot to wellness and meditation made him an unusual figure in drill. His 'Cottonwood 2' mixtape shows the range.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Shotta Flow' — the rapid-fire flow that launched him at seventeen. Notice how the energy never drops for the whole song.

name: Los Tigres del Norte
teaser: The norteño legends who sing the immigrant experience: 'La Jaula de Oro', 'El Circo', 'Jefe de Jefes' — four generations of Tigres have made corridos about migration, drugs and family the conscience of the Mexican-American border. They are the most successful band in Latin music history.

exploreAction.targetName: Los Tigres del Norte — La Jaula de Oro (1984) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'La Jaula de Oro' — the song about the gilded cage of the American dream. Notice how the accordion and the bajo sexto carry the story.

name: Christian Nodal
teaser: The young king of mariachi: 'Adiós Amor', 'Probablemente', 'De Los Besos Que Te Di' — Nodal revived the traditional mariachi-ranchera sound at nineteen and became the genre's biggest star of the 2010s. His fusion of old-school mariachi with modern production made him a phenomenon.

exploreAction.targetName: Christian Nodal — Me Dejé Llevar (2017) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Adiós Amor' — the breakup anthem that put him on top. Notice how the mariachi arrangement is authentic and the voice is completely modern.

name: José José
teaser: El Príncipe de la Canción: 'El Triste', 'Gavilán o Paloma', 'Amar y Querer' — José José's velvet baritone made him the greatest romantic ballad singer in Latin history. His vocal control and his tragic story — the voice destroyed by alcohol — made him a legend.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'El Triste' — the performance that made him a superstar. Notice how his voice moves through three octaves with total control.

name: Marco Antonio Solís
teaser: El Buki: the songwriter behind Los Bukis and a solo career of romantic ballads — 'Si No Te Hubieras Ido', 'Más Que Tu Amigo', 'La Pareja Ideal' — Solís's gruff, heartfelt voice and his catalog of heartbreak made him the most beloved romantic singer in Latin America.

exploreAction.targetName: Marco Antonio Solís — Más de Mi Alma (2001) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Si No Te Hubieras Ido' — the classic about regret. Notice how the mariachi builds under his voice at the chorus.

name: Femi Kuti
teaser: The Afrobeat heir: Fela's eldest son has carried the torch for Afrobeat and its politics since the nineties — 'Truth Don Die', 'Sorry Sorry', 'One People One World' — with his band Positive Force and his own shrine in Lagos. He has been nominated for Grammys four times.

exploreAction.targetName: Femi Kuti — Africa for Africa (2011) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Truth Don Die' — the political funk anthem. Notice how the horns and the two-hour-plus groove keep Fela's sound alive.

name: Seun Kuti
teaser: The youngest Kuti: Fela's son took over the Egypt 80 band at fourteen and has kept Afrobeat radical — 'Black Times', 'African Dreams', 'Struggle Sounds' — with an even harder political edge. His album with Black Thought is a generational meeting.

exploreAction.targetName: Seun Kuti & Egypt 80 — Black Times (2018) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the title track — the funk fury with the political lyrics. Notice how the band keeps the classic Afrobeat shape while adding modern production.

name: Orchestra Baobab
teaser: The Senegalese-Cuban fusion pioneers: their 1970s sound blended Afro-Cuban son with Senegalese Wolof and Mandinka melodies — 'Utru Horas', 'Goulade', 'Hommage à Tonton Ferrer' — and their 2001 reunion album 'Specialist in All Styles' (produced by Youssou N'Dour) is a masterpiece.

exploreAction.targetName: Orchestra Baobab — Specialist in All Styles (2002) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Utru Horas' — the salsa-senegalese groove. Notice how the Cuban tres guitar and the African percussion lock into the same rhythm.

name: Toumani Diabaté
teaser: The kora virtuoso: from Mali's great griot family, Diabaté's twenty-one-string kora playing — 'The Mande Variations', 'Ali Farka Touré duets', 'New Ancient Strings' — redefined what the instrument could do. His albums with Taj Mahal and Björk brought the kora to the world.

exploreAction.targetName: Toumani Diabaté — The Mande Variations (2008) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the title track — the solo kora album recorded in one take. Notice how the twenty-one strings create both melody and rhythm simultaneously.

name: Rokia Traoré
teaser: The Malian singer-guitarist who modernized griot song: 'Mouneïssa', 'Tchwa', 'Beautiful Africa' — Traoré's own compositions, sung in Bambara with a rock-informed band, made her one of Africa's most acclaimed contemporary artists. Her 'Beau Comme le Soleil' won France's Victoire award.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Mouneïssa' — the album's centerpiece about exile. Notice how her voice, high and precise, floats over the sparse, modern arrangement.

name: Vieux Farka Touré
teaser: The Hendrix of the Sahara: Ali Farka Touré's son carries the desert blues into the electric age — 'Allah', 'L'Exode', 'Les Racines' — playing with a fire his father reserved for the gods. His collaborations with Dave Matthews and John Scofield prove the sound travels.

exploreAction.targetName: Vieux Farka Touré — The Secret (2011) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Allah' — the tribute to his father, recorded with Ali's final tapes. Notice how his electric guitar bends and wails over the hypnotic rhythm.

name: Bassekou Kouyaté
teaser: The ngoni revolutionary: Kouyaté's six-string hunter's harp, amplified and electric, made his group Ngoni Ba the most exciting band in Malian music — 'Segou Blue', 'Ba Power' — blending griot tradition with funk and blues. He is the reason the ngoni is a rock instrument.

exploreAction.targetName: Bassekou Kouyaté & Ngoni Ba — I Speak Fula (2009) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Sira' — the ngoni playing the bass and the lead at once. Notice how the traditional griot praise-singing rides the electric groove.

name: The Offspring
teaser: The suburban punk pranksters: 'Pretty Fly (for a White Guy)', 'Self Esteem', 'The Kids Aren't Alright' — the Offspring's pop-punk singalongs sold over 40 million records and put punk on the mainstream map of the nineties. Dexter Holland, a Ph.D. candidate in molecular biology, wrote 'Come Out and Play' while studying.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Self Esteem' — the anthem about being walked all over. Notice how the band's speed and the sardonic lyrics made them the thinking kid's punk band.

name: Bad Religion
teaser: The intellectual punk institution: 'American Jesus', 'Sorrow', '21st Century (Digital Boy)' — Greg Graffin's three-part harmonies and his Ph.D.-level lyrics made Bad Religion punk's philosophy department. Thirty-plus years and twenty albums later, they remain the genre's conscience.

exploreAction.targetName: Bad Religion — Recipe for Hate (1993) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'American Jesus' — the anti-idolatry anthem with the soaring chorus. Notice how the harmonies make the anger beautiful.

name: NOFX
teaser: The skate-punk pranksters: 'Linoleum', 'The Separation of Church and Skate', 'Bob' — Fat Mike's band built a three-decade career on self-deprecating humor, drug jokes and tight, fast punk. Their 1994 album 'Punk in Drublic' is the genre's landmark.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Linoleum' — the four-chord anthem about being broke and free. Notice how the band's humor hides real songwriting craft.

name: Rancid
teaser: The Bay Area street punk revival: 'Time Bomb', 'Ruby Soho', 'Fall Back Down' — Tim Armstrong and Lars Frederiksen's two-front attack made Rancid the heirs to the Clash, mixing ska, reggae and hardcore into a punk melting pot. Their '...And Out Come the Wolves' is the genre's crossover classic.

exploreAction.targetName: Rancid — ...And Out Come the Wolves (1995) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Time Bomb' — the ska-punk anthem with the walking bassline. Notice how the twin vocalists trade lines like a conversation.

name: Stone Temple Pilots
teaser: The grunge survivors who outgrew the label: 'Plush', 'Interstate Love Song', 'Sour Girl' — Scott Weiland's chameleon voice and the DeLeo brothers' songwriting made STP the most versatile band of the grunge era. Their 'Purple' and 'Tiny Music' albums show the range critics denied them.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Interstate Love Song' — the melancholy hit that defined their sound. Notice how Weiland's delivery shifts between whisper and howl.

name: Goo Goo Dolls
teaser: The Buffalo alt-rockers who became ballad kings: 'Iris', 'Name', 'Slide' — John Rzeznik's husky voice and the band's power-ballad heart made 'Dizzy Up the Girl' one of the biggest albums of 1998. 'Iris' spent 18 weeks at number one on the adult charts.

exploreAction.targetName: Goo Goo Dolls — Dizzy Up the Girl (1998) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Iris' — the song written for City of Angels with its 18-week chart run. Notice how the strings and the electric guitar build into the chorus.

name: Third Eye Blind
teaser: The nineties alt-pop perfectionists: 'Semi-Charmed Life', 'Jumper', 'How's It Going to Be' — Stephan Jenkins' wordy, sunny-sinister songs made their self-titled debut a multi-platinum classic. 'Semi-Charmed Life' — about crystal meth, disguised as a summer anthem — is the era's great Trojan horse.

exploreAction.targetName: Third Eye Blind — Third Eye Blind (1997) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Semi-Charmed Life' — the catchy hit with the darkest lyrics of 1997. Notice how the band's harmonies and the driving guitar hide the subject.

name: Matchbox Twenty
teaser: The nineties adult-alternative kings: 'Push', '3AM', 'Unwell' — Rob Thomas' raspy voice and the band's big choruses made 'Yourself or Someone Like You' one of the best-selling albums of the decade. Thomas's 'Smooth' with Santana added a global hit.

exploreAction.targetName: Matchbox Twenty — Yourself or Someone Like You (1996) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Push' — the controversial hit about a manipulative relationship. Notice how the band's dynamics make the verses feel conversational.

name: Bush
teaser: The British grunge imports: 'Glycerine', 'Machinehead', 'Everything Zen' — Gavin Rossdale's band rode the grunge wave to global success with their debut 'Sixteen Stone'. Their brooding, hooky alt-rock made them one of the biggest bands of the mid-nineties.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Glycerine' — the stripped-back ballad that became a wedding song. Notice how the quiet verses contrast with the roaring choruses.

name: Silverchair
teaser: The teenage grunge prodigies from Australia: 'Tomorrow', 'Freak', 'Ana's Song' — Silverchair's debut was written when Daniel Johns was fourteen, and their evolution from grunge to orchestral art-rock ('Diorama') proved they were never just a teen sensation. Johns is now one of Australia's most respected songwriters.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Tomorrow' — the grunge anthem written by a fourteen-year-old. Notice how the album's production, by the band's parents' generation, frames the teenage fury.

name: DJ Shadow
teaser: The sample-collage pioneer: 'Endtroducing.....' — built entirely from dusty vinyl samples, recorded in a small bedroom — is the most influential instrumental hip-hop album ever. 'Midnight in a Perfect World' and 'Building Steam with a Grain of Salt' turned crate-digging into an art form.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Midnight in a Perfect World' — the record that made instrumental hip-hop a genre. Notice how the samples feel like a film score for a movie that doesn't exist.

name: Orbital
teaser: The techno brothers: Phil and Paul Hartnoll's 'Chime' and their 'Halcyon' — with its famous sample of 'It's a Fine Day' — defined UK techno's melodic, euphoric sound. Their Glastonbury sunrise sets and their 'Orbital 2' album (the green one) are electronic music canon.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Halcyon' — the eleven-minute masterpiece with the 'On and On' vocal sample. Notice how the track builds and releases like waves.

name: Underworld
teaser: The dance music philosophers: 'Born Slippy .NUXX' — the Trainspotting anthem — and 'Rez/Cowgirl' made Karl Hyde's stream-of-consciousness vocals and Rick Smith's euphoric house the sound of nineties rave culture. Their live shows are legendary marathons.

exploreAction.targetName: Underworld — Second Toughest in the Infants (1996) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Pearl's Girl' — the album's nine-minute centerpiece. Notice how 'Born Slippy' builds its 'lager, lager, lager' chant into pure catharsis.

name: Faithless
teaser: The dance collective with the preacher's soul: 'Insomnia', 'God Is a DJ', 'We Come 1' — Sister Bliss's productions and Maxi Jazz's spoken-word vocals made Faithless the most spiritually ambitious act in dance music. 'Insomnia' remains one of the most-played dance tracks ever.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Insomnia' — the anthem built on a single piano line and a relentless beat. Notice how Maxi Jazz's voice turns the club into a sermon.

name: Goldfrapp
teaser: The shape-shifting electronic duo: Alison Goldfrapp's voice and Will Gregory's production moved from ambient folk ('Felt Mountain') to glam-electro ('Black Cherry', 'Supernature') to synth-pop ('Seventh Tree'). 'Ooh La La' and 'Ride a White Horse' defined the mid-2000s electro-clash moment.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Ooh La La' — the glam-disco stomp with the Bolan sample. Notice how the album swings between robotic electro and acoustic ballads.

name: UNKLE
teaser: The trip-hop collective of DJ Shadow and James Lavelle: 'Rabbit in Your Headlights' (with Thom Yorke) and 'Lonely Soul' (with Richard Ashcroft) made their debut 'Psyence Fiction' the post-Rave landmark of 1998. Their rotating cast has kept the project alive for two decades.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Rabbit in Your Headlights' — the Thom Yorke collaboration with the toll-booth story. Notice how the trip-hop beat builds into a string-laden climax.

name: Mura Masa
teaser: The Guernsey producer who made the internet a genre: 'Love$ick', 'Firefly', 'Live Like We're Dancing' — Alex Crossan's blend of future bass, garage and pop made him the leading producer of the 2010s online generation. His debut album won the Ivor Novello for best electronic work.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Love$ick' — the A$AP Rocky collaboration built on a garage sample. Notice how the production is clean, digital and unmistakably modern.

name: Troye Sivan
teaser: The Australian pop star who turned vulnerability into an aesthetic: 'Youth', 'Bloom', 'Angel Baby' — Troye's confessional lyrics and his queer-forward pop made him a global icon for his generation. His 'Something to Give Each Other' album is his boldest work.

exploreAction.targetName: Troye Sivan — Something to Give Each Other (2023) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Rush' — the house-influenced hit about queer joy. Notice how the album balances euphoria and melancholy without dropping the beat.

name: Kim Petras
teaser: The German pop machine: 'Heart to Break', 'Malibu', 'Unholy' — Petras made history as the first openly trans woman to top the Billboard Hot 100 (with Sam Smith's 'Unholy'). Her bubblegum pop and her 'Turn Off the Light' horror-pop album showed the range.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Heart to Break' — the hyperpop-tinged heartbreak anthem. Notice how the production keeps the melody front and center.

name: Rina Sawayama
teaser: The Japanese-British boundary breaker: 'STFU!', 'XS', 'SAWAYAMA' — Rina's debut fused nu-metal, pop and R&B with a sharp critique of consumerism and identity. Her 'Hold the Girl' follow-up and her role in John Wick 4 confirmed the multi-hyphenate reach.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'STFU!' — the nu-metal pop fusion with the confrontational chorus. Notice how the album jumps genres every track without losing cohesion.

name: Ellie Goulding
teaser: The ethereal voice of 2010s pop: 'Lights', 'Burn', 'Love Me Like You Do' — Goulding's fluttering soprano and her electro-folk blend made her one of the decade's most streamed artists. Her 'Fifty Shades' hit and her 'Halcyon' album anchored her mainstream reign.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Anything Could Happen' — the soaring opener. Notice how the production by Skrillex and others gives her voice an electronic halo.

name: Wiz Khalifa
teaser: The Pittsburgh weed-rap icon: 'Black and Yellow', 'See You Again', 'Young Wild & Free' — Wiz's easygoing flow and his association with the green made him one of the most successful rappers of the 2010s. 'See You Again' (for Furious 7) became one of the most-streamed songs in history.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Black and Yellow' — the hometown anthem that became a sports staple. Notice how the minimal production lets his relaxed flow carry everything.

name: Machine Gun Kelly
teaser: The rapper who became a pop-punk star: 'Bad Things', 'bloody valentine', 'my ex's best friend' — MGK's pivot from rap to pop-punk with 'Tickets to My Downfall' made him the biggest rock debut of 2020. His rap roots ('Rage Pack', 'Hotel Diablo') still anchor his sound.

exploreAction.targetName: Machine Gun Kelly — Tickets to My Downfall (2020) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'bloody valentine' — the emo-pop crossover that defined the album. Notice how the Travis Barker production gives it authentic punk drums.

name: French Montana
teaser: The Moroccan-born New York rapper: 'Pop That', 'Unforgettable', 'No Stylist' — French's hooky, melodic trap and his 'Unforgettable' (with Swae Lee) made him a global star. His coke-boy aesthetic and his marathon mixtape run ('Coke Boys') defined his brand.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Unforgettable' — the afrobeat-tinged smash with Swae Lee. Notice how the song's chorus is the whole hit, repeated to hypnotic effect.

name: Tyga
teaser: The West Coast hit machine: 'Rack City', 'Taste', 'Ayy Macarena' — Tyga's club-ready singles and his cameo-heavy videos made him a consistent chart presence for a decade. His 'Careless World' album and his features kept him in the conversation.

exploreAction.targetName: Tyga — Careless World: Rise of the Last King (2012) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Rack City' — the minimal, bass-heavy anthem. Notice how the hook is designed for maximum repetition and minimum effort.

name: Lil Tecca
teaser: The teenage viral phenomenon: 'Ransom', 'Did It Again', 'Never Left' — Tecca's debut mixtape went platinum on the strength of 'Ransom', a minimalist trap earworm recorded at sixteen. His 'Virgo World' album proved the staying power.

exploreAction.targetName: Lil Tecca — We Love You Tecca (2019) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Ransom' — the beat that broke the internet. Notice how his relaxed, off-hand delivery makes the whole thing feel effortless.

name: Julien Baker
teaser: The confessional indie-rock voice: 'Sprained Ankle', 'Appointments', 'Faith Healer' — recorded alone in a church, Julien Baker's debut made her the most devastating songwriter of the 2010s indie scene. Her work with boygenius and her solo albums map faith, addiction and recovery.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the title track — the album opener recorded in one take. Notice how the guitar and her voice carry everything with no adornment.

name: Lucy Dacus
teaser: The novelist of indie rock: 'Night Shift', 'VBS', 'Thumbs' — Dacus's 'Historian' and 'Home Video' albums turned personal history into universal art with a literary precision rare in music. Her 'Thumbs' live performance is the most shared moment of the band's boygenius tour.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Thumbs' — the seven-minute song about watching someone stand up to their abuser. Notice how the band builds from a whisper to a roar and back.

name: DIIV
teaser: The shoegaze revivalists of Brooklyn: 'Doused', 'Under the Sun', 'Blankenship' — Zachary Cole Smith's band took the genre's swirling guitars into the 2010s and made 'Oshin' and 'Deceiver' landmarks of the revival. Their live shows are walls of sound.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Blankenship' — the album's most anthemic moment. Notice how the fuzz guitars and the driving rhythm section make sadness feel powerful.

name: The Story So Far
teaser: The modern pop-punk standard: 'Quicksand', 'Nerve', 'Out of It' — Parker Cannon's shouted, melodic vocals and the band's tight, technical pop-punk made 'Under Soil and Dirt' and 'Proper Dose' era-defining. They are the template for every band in the 2010s scene.

exploreAction.targetName: The Story So Far — Proper Dose (2018) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to 'Out of It' — the song about getting through. Notice how the band's evolution from hardcore-leaning pop-punk to mature songwriting is complete here.

name: Neck Deep
